summary: This Britannica entry defines split-brain syndrome as a set of neurological abnormalities caused by partial or complete severing or lesioning of the corpus callosum, the nerve bundle linking the brain's two hemispheres. It explains the specialized roles of each hemisphere, outlines causes including corpus callosotomy for severe epilepsy and less common stroke, tumour, multiple sclerosis or agenesis, and describes symptoms such as preserved memory and motor skills, impaired bimanual tasks, and difficulty naming objects held in the left hand or odours in the right nostril.
one_line: Britannica entry on split-brain syndrome, a neurological condition from severing or damage to the corpus callosum that makes the brain's hemispheres function independently.
key_facts: Split-brain syndrome is a condition characterized by a cluster of neurological abnormalities arising from the partial or complete severing or lesioning of the corpus callosum.
The corpus callosum is the bundle of nerves that connects the right and left hemispheres of the brain.
Roger Wolcott Sperry, an American neurobiologist, was among the first to characterize split-brain syndrome and studied human split-brain subjects in the 1960s.
Roger Wolcott Sperry received a share of the 1981 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine for this work.
The primary cause of split-brain syndrome is intentional severing of the corpus callosum through a surgical procedure known as corpus callosotomy.
Corpus callosotomy is reserved as a last measure of treatment for extreme and uncontrollable forms of epilepsy in which violent seizures spread from one side of the brain to the other.
Less-common causes of split-brain syndrome include stroke, infectious lesion, tumour, or ruptured artery.
The syndrome can also be caused by multiple sclerosis and in rare instances by agenesis of the corpus callosum.
Split-brain patients retain intact memory and social skills and maintain motor skills learned before onset, such as walking, swimming, and biking.
Split-brain patients cannot learn new tasks requiring interdependent movement of each hand, such as learning to play the piano.
Eye movements remain coordinated in split-brain patients.
A blindfolded split-brain patient may not be able to name a familiar object held in the left hand because touch information goes to the right hemisphere, which typically has a weak language centre.
Patients are unable to name odours presented to the right nostril, though the left hand can point out the source.
The left hemisphere is generally responsible for analytical tasks such as calculating and reading, and is dominant for speech and language in many individuals.
Split-brain syndrome is associated with alien-hand syndrome, characterized by involuntary and uncoordinated yet purposeful movement of the hands.
